summary: Every Arabic noun is masculine or feminine. Most feminine nouns end in tāʾ marbūṭa ـة (غُرْفَة، شَقَّة، طَاوِلَة); nouns for women are feminine whatever their ending (بِنْت، أُمّ); and some nouns are feminine with no ة at all — كَأْس (glass), دَار (house), شَمْس (sun), أَرْض (earth), and body parts that come in pairs (يَد، عَيْن، رِجْل). Everything else is masculine. Gender decides “this” (هٰذَا / هٰذِهِ), “it” (هُوَ / هِيَ), and later adjectives and verbs. Nouns for people come in pairs: طَالِب / طَالِبَة, مُعَلِّم / مُعَلِّمَة.

blocks.title: People: a masculine and a feminine.
blocks.text: طَالِب → طَالِبَة, مُعَلِّم → مُعَلِّمَة, صَدِيق → صَدِيقَة: add ة. Plurals: طُلَّاب / طَالِبَات, مُعَلِّمُونَ / مُعَلِّمَات, أَصْدِقَاء / صَدِيقَات. A mixed group takes the masculine plural.

blocks.title: Masculine with ة.
blocks.text: A few masculine nouns end in ة: خَلِيفَة (caliph), and men’s names such as حَمْزَة and أُسَامَة. The meaning (a man) wins.

blocks.title: Test with “this” and “it”.
blocks.text: Not sure? Use the noun with هٰذَا / هٰذِهِ or answer with هُوَ / هِيَ: هٰذِهِ كَأْسٌ — الْكَأْسُ؟ هِيَ هُنَا.
A collective noun (وَرَق paper, بَصَل onions) is masculine; its unit noun in ة is feminine: وَرَق → وَرَقَة (a sheet of paper).
مَاء (water) ends in -āʾ but is masculine: its hamza belongs to the root, it is not the feminine ending.

askYourself: Does it end in ـة? → feminine (unless it names a man: خَلِيفَة).
Does it name a woman or a girl? → feminine.
Is it one of the feminines without ة (كَأْس، دَار، شَمْس، أَرْض، نَار) or a paired body part? → feminine.
Does it end in the feminine -āʾ / -ā (صَحْرَاء، كُبْرَى)? → feminine — but مَاء is masculine.

traps: كَأْس is feminine: هٰذِهِ كَأْسٌ, not *هٰذَا كَأْسٌ.
بِنْت ends in ت, not ة — and is feminine.
Plurals of things agree as feminine singular whatever the gender of the singular: كِتَاب (m.) → هٰذِهِ الْكُتُبُ.
The same thing often has another gender in your other languages: بَيْت is masculine (das Haus is neuter), شَمْس is feminine (ο ήλιος is masculine).

quiz.why: One of the feminines without ة: هٰذِهِ كَأْسٌ.
No ة, not a woman, not on the list of exceptions → masculine.
The others are feminine: two end in ة, and بِنْت is a girl.
كَأْس is feminine; no article → a sentence.

seeAlso.note: Hebrew has the same two genders and the same main sign (feminine -ָה / -ֶת), with feminines that lack it (אֶרֶץ, earth) — and כּוֹס (glass) is feminine there too.
German has three genders that the form rarely shows — learn der / die / das with every noun; Arabic gender is mostly visible (ة).
Chinese nouns have no gender; he / she / it differ only in the writing (他 / 她 / 它).
